title: A contact path for a manufacturer
metaTitle: A manufacturer contact page that replies
excerpt: Say who replies, how soon, and what to have ready. Offer a spec download beside a short form. Ten required fields will lose the buyer you just convinced.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops, for a piece on handing a buyer to the right person.
caption: A working table, with someone directing the next step. A contact page should be that explicit. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a manufacturer contact page say first?
faqs.answer: What happens after the note is sent. Who reads it, what the first reply contains, and the window you already keep. A spec download belongs on the same screen for buyers who are not ready to talk. Mystery is not a professional tone.

faqs.question: How many form fields are enough?
faqs.answer: A way to reply, the company, and a sentence about the part, plus an optional file. Phone, ship-to region, and intent can be added when you will use them. Budget, job title, and how they heard of you are research. Collect those later, if at all.

faqs.question: Should the page promise a response time?
faqs.answer: Only if the shop already meets it. Say the window in business days and name the clock. A same-day promise that becomes a week of silence is worse than a true, slower sentence. Fix the queue before you publish the number of days.

markdown:
A manufacturer contact page tells a buyer who needs specs and confidence what happens after they reach out, how soon they will hear back, and what to have ready. The action is to talk to sales or download a spec. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them, especially when a shorter path would have started a useful conversation.

Write this page as a handoff. The buyer is leaving their own work and entering yours. They should know who receives them, what the first reply contains, and which file will make that reply smarter. Mystery is not a professional tone. It is a reason to try the next supplier on the list.

## Say what happens next

The first lines under the heading should describe the handoff in order. You send a drawing or a question. A named role reads it. You get a reply that says whether the job fits, what is missing, and how a quote or a sample would proceed. That is enough structure for a buyer to feel the path is real.

Name the role. "Applications engineering reads new drawings" is better than "our team will be in touch." If several people share the queue, say that, and say who is accountable when the note is about fit. A buyer with a hard tolerance wants to know the note will not die in a general inbox.

Describe the first reply. Fit, a request for one missing fact, or a clear no when the work sits outside your boundary. A clear no is a service. It returns the buyer's time. Promise it, and mean it. A contact path that only knows how to say "absolutely, let's hop on a call" will clog with work you should have declined on the page.

If a spec download will answer the question faster, offer it above the form. Many visitors on this page are not ready to talk. They want the file. Forcing a conversation before the file is available trains them to leave. Put the download beside the form, with one sentence on what the file contains and its revision.

## What to have ready

List the materials that change the quality of the first reply. A drawing or model, the material if they are specifying it, the annual or batch quantity, the date they need parts, and the characteristic they are worried about. Four or five items. The list is guidance. It should not all be required fields.

Mark what is required with restraint. A way to reach them, and a sentence about the part, may be enough to start. The drawing can be attached or sent as a link. If you require a file to quote, say that quotes need a file, and still let them ask a fit question without one. Two intents can share a page if the form makes the intent obvious. "I have a drawing" and "I have a fit question" can be a first choice that shortens the rest.

Say which formats you can open. STEP, a dimensioned PDF, a native file you actually support. "Any format" is rarely true and leads to a reply that asks them to export again. State the limit. Also state any limit on file size, and what to do when the pack is larger. A shared link is a reasonable fallback. Write the fallback on the page so they do not invent a workaround in the body of an email that your form then rejects.

Tell them what not to include only when it protects them. Full pricing from their current supplier, unrelated personal data, export-controlled files if you are not the right recipient. A short caution is professional. A legal wall before the form is a deterrent. Put the necessary notice where it can be read, and keep it in language a person can finish.

## A short form

The form itself should look like the list. Name, company, email, the intent, a message, an optional file. Phone if you will use it. Country or ship-to region if it changes fit. Stop there. Dropdowns for budget, timeline, how you heard of us, job title, and company size are research questions. They are not the buyer's job. Collect them later, if you still want them, after you have earned the conversation.

Write labels that stay visible. Placeholder text that disappears is how people submit blank confusion. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats understandable input as part of an accessible page: labels, help, and a way to recover from errors. That is also the right standard for a busy engineer. Label every field in text. When something is wrong, say what it is and keep what they already typed.

Show errors next to the field. "Add an email so we can reply" is enough. A banner at the top that says the form failed, without saying where, is how people resubmit the same mistake or leave. On success, say what will happen and how soon, and offer the spec download again in case they still want it. A blank thank-you page with no next step wastes the moment.

Test the form with a real file. Send a drawing from a phone and from a laptop. Check the spam folder of the receiving inbox. Check that the attachment arrives, that the from-address is readable, and that a person is responsible for the queue when the usual person is out. A contact page that works only on the day it was demoed is a broken page.

## How fast, stated as a window you keep

Publish a response window you already meet. If new drawings get a first look within two business days, say two business days. If the window is longer when a file needs a toolmaker's eyes, say that too. The damage comes from a promise of an hour because it sounded attentive, followed by a silence of a week.

State the clock. Business days, the time zone of the plant, and what happens on holidays if that is when your buyers write. A global buyer will send notes on your weekend. You do not have to staff the weekend. You do have to say when the clock runs, so their expectation matches the shop.

If you miss the window often, fix the queue before you publish the sentence. The page cannot compensate for an inbox nobody owns. Assign the owner, name a backup, and then publish. The sentence is an operations commitment that marketing happens to display.

Auto-replies are fine when they repeat the window and the list of what helps, and when a human follows. An auto-reply that says a coordinator will reach out, with no coordinator, is the ten-field form in a different costume. Keep the automation short and true.

## Who receives the message

Say where the message goes, in human terms. A sales inbox that applications engineering reads. A person, if the company is small enough that a person is true. Give an alternate path for an existing order, so current customers do not use the new-business form for a late shipment. Those are different queues. Mixing them is how urgent notes wait behind cold inquiries, and how new buyers wait behind emergencies.

Publish a phone number only if the behavior matches the page. If the number is answered or returned in the same window, it can sit beside the form. If it is a switchboard that cannot talk about a drawing, leave it off this page and put the right number on the packing list and the invoice, where existing customers look.

An address belongs here when visits and shipments are part of the relationship. Write it as text. Add the note about whether you accept visitors, and how a visit gets booked. An unannounced lobby full of people who "saw the address on the site" is an operations problem you can prevent with one sentence.

Privacy copy should say what you will do with a drawing. You will use it to judge fit and to quote. You will not add them to a newsletter because they asked for a quote. If you want marketing mail, ask separately, and accept no as the default. Buyers notice the checkbox that opts them in by surprise. It colors the whole path.

## The page around the form

Keep the contact page consistent with the offer. One line on what you make, the boundary that most often matters, and the links to the spec and to a proof. A buyer who landed here from search may not have seen the homepage. Give them enough to know they are in the right plant, and do not make them read the whole site before the form.

Repeat the boundary that saves wasted inquiries. Materials, minimums, the work you do not take. This is not a second services page. It is a filter for people who are about to write. A sentence with a link to the fuller list is the right weight.

The confirmation and the error states are part of the design. Review them in the same session as the hero of the homepage. A careful first screen followed by a broken form is the experience the buyer will remember. On a Hanabi project the form is built with the page, in the repository, so the labels and the destination inbox are not a plugin someone is afraid to touch. You should be able to change the window, the fields, and the receiving address without a redesign.

## Try the path before you announce it

Send three test inquiries. A complete drawing. A fit question with no file. A request that should be declined. Confirm the replies match the page: the window, the owner, the willingness to say no. Fix the replies or fix the page until they match. Then ask sales if they would forward this URL to a good prospect. If they hesitate, the page is still doing something that makes them look unreliable.

Remove fields until the hesitation goes away. The usual extras are the ones nobody reads. Budget, website, job title, a mandatory phone number. Each required field is a small door. Ten of them make a corridor. Two or three make a handoff.

Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) if you want to see how a public site can keep a next step specific and quiet. The same restraint belongs on a contact page. A clear handoff, a short form, a spec beside it.

After the path works, the useful question is what should never have been on the site at all. [What not to put on the site for a manufacturer](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-manufacturer) is the next piece, because a factory cliché with no product still confuses the buyer you just made it easy to reach.
